clauses.title: 5.1 Be honest about limits: do not claim a host's bare shell was locked when that host exposes no hook surface the guard can attach to.
5.2 Prefer reversible steps and surface the blast radius of an action before taking it.
5.3 Keep the runtime to the Python standard library. Optional third-party deps, if any, go in requirements.txt and are never required to run the gates.
5.4 Leave a clear, auditable trail: what was decided, why, and what was verified.
5.5 Completion is a stage, not a feeling: every deliverable sits on one of five stages — S0 chartered (10%), S1 in progress (35%), S2 runnable (65%), S3 accepted (90%), S4 archived (100%).
body: The percentage is derived from the stage, never typed in by hand. A stage change that only ever goes up is treated as falsified bookkeeping.

S0 requires a project record stating goal, boundary and deliverable. S1 requires working material but no usable artifact. S2 requires an artifact that actually opens and is non-empty. S3 requires the client to say so — without that, S2 is the ceiling. S4 requires the whole directory to have moved into 90_lishi, with nothing left in place.
Every delivery note must carry one line: 'Stage: S? (evidence: ...)'. Missing that line counts as not delivered.

clauses.title: 5.6 Two healths, judged apart: host health (A) covers the machine — drivers, services, disk, ports, shortcuts, locked files; system health (B) covers the rule engine itself — version, clause count, gate results, defect ledger, schedule, work log.
body: They are never blended into one score. A single 'health score' hides exactly the thing you need to act on.

Each side declares its own closing criteria. A rule of thumb: A closes when no P0 item remains and the disk has room for three times the expected output; B closes when every gate passes, the defect ledger has no open row, and today's work log is written.
Only when both sides close may you say 'closed' and archive a batch. Otherwise list the open items by id — 'basically fine' is not a status.
Allowed status words: normal / pending-reboot / open / closed. Inventing a fifth word is a rules bypass.

clauses.title: 5.7 Machine judgement is a baseline, not the final word: a human override may change how a task or project is displayed, and it must be recorded with who and when.
body: Two layers: the baseline computed from disk and ledgers, and the override written by a human. Display prefers the override and keeps the baseline visible so it can be restored in one click.
Override keys must be stable identifiers — a file path for a task, an abbreviation for a project. Never a title: titles change, and the override silently disappears with them.
An override never bypasses a gate. Marking a task 'done' does not turn a failing check green. Using an override as evidence is a rules bypass.
If the override file is corrupt, degrade to 'no override' and say so; never swallow the error.

clauses.title: 5.8 Daily work log is mandatory: one row per delivery, six columns — date, time, actor, task, what was done, pointer to the full record.
body: The pointer must resolve to a file that actually exists. A row pointing at nothing counts as not logged.
The log is an index, not a report. Process, evidence and review live in the file being pointed at; the log never duplicates the body.
Rolling retention (90 days by default): expired rows move to an archive subdirectory. Never delete a row, never rewrite a historical date.
This framework does not ship the gate that enforces it; adopters implement 'zero rows today = FAIL' in their own engine and register it under 4.2 of their map.
